title: Sell Mineral Rights in Pennsylvania
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Pennsylvania | Marcellus Gas Royalties
metaDescription: Pennsylvania mineral owner? The Marcellus is a gas play, not oil. Learn how gas royalties actually get valued here before you consider a sale.
heroLead: Let's be straightforward about it: Pennsylvania is a natural gas state, not an oil state, and any conversation about your minerals should start from that fact.
intro: Pennsylvania's modern mineral wealth comes almost entirely from the Marcellus shale, one of the largest natural gas fields in the world, running through counties like Washington, Greene, Susquehanna, and Bradford. Deeper Utica shale gas adds a second layer in parts of the state. There's a small historical footnote worth knowing: the world's first commercial oil well was drilled near Titusville in 1859, and pockets of very old, shallow oil production still exist in northwestern counties like Venango and McKean, but that's a tiny fraction of what Pennsylvania minerals are worth today compared to Marcellus gas.

If you're holding a Pennsylvania interest and wondering whether to sell, the real question is almost always about a gas royalty's decline pattern and pricing, not an oil decline curve, so this page focuses on getting that part right.

sections.heading: How a Marcellus gas well declines
paragraphs: Marcellus wells behave similarly to other modern shale wells in one respect: they produce heavily in the first year or two, then decline into a longer, shallower tail that can run for many years. What's different from an oil well is that your royalty check moves with natural gas prices, which have their own seasonal and macro patterns separate from crude oil markets.

If your check has dropped since the well was first turned online, that's expected behavior for a maturing gas well, not necessarily a warning sign. Pulling recent check history is still the best way to understand where your specific well sits before evaluating any offer.

sections.heading: The small legacy oil pocket in northwestern Pennsylvania
paragraphs: Venango, McKean, Warren, and a handful of nearby counties still hold scattered shallow oil wells dating back over a century, remnants of the original American oil boom. These wells are typically stripper production now, small and steady, operated at a scale far removed from the Marcellus's modern industrial pace.

If your interest is one of these legacy oil tracts, don't expect it to price like a modern shale well. It will be valued on its own modest, long-running production history, which is a fundamentally different asset than a Marcellus gas royalty even though both are technically mineral interests in Pennsylvania.

sections.heading: Pennsylvania ownership and lease terms
paragraphs: Pennsylvania has a long history of severed mineral estates going back to 19th-century land transactions, meaning a lot of surface owners today don't own the minerals beneath their own land, and vice versa. Lease terms, royalty rates, and post-production cost deductions vary widely depending on when your lease was signed, with older leases sometimes carrying less favorable terms than more recent ones.

Before selling, review your lease and division order carefully, or have your attorney do so, since the specific deductions and royalty fraction written into an old Pennsylvania lease directly affect what a buyer will offer for the remaining interest.

sections.heading: What a Pennsylvania gas offer typically weighs
paragraphs: A buyer evaluating your Marcellus interest will ask for recent check stubs, your division order, and details on whether your unit sits in an active drilling area or one where development has largely wound down. Counties like Washington and Greene have seen more continuous activity than some of the more rural northern tier counties, which can affect how much remaining upside a buyer is willing to price in.

Post-production costs, meaning the deductions taken for gathering, compression, and transportation before your royalty is calculated, can vary meaningfully between leases and directly affect your net check, so understanding your specific deduction structure helps you judge whether an offer reflects your true production accurately.

faqs.question: Is Pennsylvania an oil state or a gas state?
faqs.answer: Overwhelmingly gas today. The Marcellus and deeper Utica shale produce natural gas across most of the state. A small amount of legacy oil production remains in northwestern counties, but it's a minor share of overall value.

faqs.question: Why did my Pennsylvania royalty check drop after the first couple of years?
faqs.answer: Marcellus gas wells decline steeply in their early years before settling into a longer, shallower tail, similar to shale oil wells elsewhere. A declining then leveling check is typical, not unusual.

faqs.question: Does my old Pennsylvania lease affect what I'd get for selling?
faqs.answer: Yes. Royalty rate and post-production cost deductions vary by lease vintage, and both directly affect the net value of your interest. Review your lease terms, or have your attorney review them, before comparing offers.

faqs.question: Do I own the minerals under my own land in Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Pennsylvania has a long history of severed mineral estates, so it's common for surface and mineral ownership to belong to different parties. Your deed history will clarify this.

faqs.question: What are post-production cost deductions?
faqs.answer: Charges for gathering, compressing, and transporting gas before it reaches market, deducted from your royalty under many Pennsylvania leases. The exact deduction structure varies by lease and affects your net check.
